_about: Chip map for the Hey Sparky project page (site/chip/chipview.js through tools/render_projects.py t_chip_panel). Not a board page file, so the board page and the Digital Lab ignore it. Every row traces to ports/xiaozhi/target-cc35x1: xz_main.c (the turn, the button, Wi-Fi), xz_audio.c (the ADC, the timer, the DAC lines), xz_ws.c (WebSocket on TCP), xz_wake.cc (wake word), xz_lcd.c and xz_screen.syscfg (SPI0, DMA, software I2C touch). Header pins are checked against data/boardviz/cc35x1.json and the sizes against data/results/cc35x1.csv (xiaozhi rows) by tools/chip_jobs_project_check.py. chip.ram_bytes is the RAM the linker can place data in (data/results/cc35x1.csv, doom-s3-zone and its static rows: 491,520 + 131,071 + 32,768 + 27,748). chip.flash_bytes is the 2,696 kB application slot.

cpu.name: Cortex-M33 CPU
cpu.note: 32-bit Arm Cortex-M33 at 160 MHz in the CC3551E

flash.name: Flash
flash.note: The program lives in the 8 MB flash chip on the board; this build takes 1,577 kB of its 2,696 kB application slot

sram.name: SRAM
sram.note: Static RAM of the voice image; a 319 kB FreeRTOS heap for task stacks sits beside it

clk.name: Clocks and power
clk.sub: 160 MHz CPU, 80 MHz timer clock, 3.3 V
clk.note: The CPU runs at 160 MHz; the general-purpose timer counts at 80 MHz

adc0.name: ADC0
adc0.note: 12-bit converter that reads the microphone pin

gpt.name: General timer
gpt.note: General-purpose timer whose interrupt sets the 16 kHz sample rate

gpio.name: GPIO
gpio.note: Digital pins: the button, the DAC's three lines, touch, screen control

spi0.name: SPI0
spi0.note: Serial bus that carries pixels to the screen

dma.name: DMA
dma.note: Moves the pixels to the SPI block without the CPU

wifi.name: Wi-Fi 6 radio
wifi.note: The Wi-Fi radio and its network stack carry the WebSocket to the server

ble.name: Bluetooth LE
ble.note: Used only to give the board your Wi-Fi name and password

uart2.name: UART2
uart2.note: The text console on the debug probe's serial port

wdt.name: Watchdog
wdt.note: A watchdog task restarts the board if it stops responding

sparky-voice-assistant.title: Hey Sparky voice assistant
sparky-voice-assistant.card_line: Audio pack on the LaunchPad, optional 3.5 inch screen.

dac.name: Speaker
dac.note: DAC8311, amplifier and speaker on the pack

sparky-voice-assistant.wiring: Voice alone needs no wire: the Audio BoosterPack presses onto the LaunchPad headers. The optional screen takes the 13 wires in the pin table above; S2 is on the board.

rows.step: You press S2
rows.by: S2 on the board, a pull-up input; the s key on the console or a tap on the screen does the same

rows.step: Reads the button
rows.by: GPIO, click detected by the button driver

rows.step: Starts one voice turn
rows.by: the worker task opens the connection and the microphone

rows.step: Listens for Hey Sparky
rows.by: a small neural network on every 10 ms of audio (160 samples), TensorFlow Lite Micro with CMSIS-NN kernels

rows.step: Opens the connection only after it hears it
rows.by: cutoff 230 of 255; the last 960 ms, kept as 8-bit samples, is sent first so the server hears the wake phrase

rows.step: The pack's microphone voltage arrives
rows.by: pack MIC OUT, header pin 6 (GPIO11), powered from GPIO10

rows.step: A timer ticks 16,000 times a second
rows.by: general-purpose timer, 80 MHz clock; its interrupt takes one sample

rows.step: Turns the voltage into a number
rows.by: ADC0, 12 bit, 0 to 3.3 V

rows.step: Removes the offset, scales it and queues it
rows.by: in the interrupt, into a ring of 8,192 16-bit samples

rows.step: Packs 60 ms of speech into an Opus packet
rows.by: Opus, CELT mode, 16 kHz mono, 24 kbit/s, complexity 0, on the CPU

rows.step: Wraps each packet in a WebSocket message
rows.by: a plain TCP socket on the Wi-Fi stack, one packet per message

rows.step: Sends it to the server over your Wi-Fi
rows.by: ws:// to port 8000 on the xiaozhi server

rows.step: Receives the reply audio
rows.by: one Opus packet per WebSocket message

rows.step: Decodes each packet
rows.by: Opus decoder at the rate the server says, 16 or 24 kHz

rows.step: Paces playback at the same rate
rows.by: the same timer, one sample per tick

rows.step: Clocks each sample into the DAC
rows.by: three lines driven by software: SYNC GPIO12, SCLK GPIO27, DIN GPIO29

rows.step: Sends the bits to the DAC8311
rows.by: pack D MOSI, header pin 15; the amplifier turns on with GPIO13 low

rows.step: Draws the look for the current state
rows.by: one strip at a time into a row buffer, then the next

rows.step: Hands the strip to the SPI block
rows.by: DMA channels 0 and 1

rows.step: Clocks the pixels out to the panel
rows.by: SPI0 at 10 MHz: MOSI on header pin 38 (GPIO19), clock on header pin 4 (GPIO17)

rows.step: A finger lands and the touch chip answers
rows.by: FT6336U at address 0x38, data on header pin 10 (GPIO32)

rows.step: Software I2C reads the position
rows.by: clock on header pin 9 (GPIO33), about 100 kHz, every 8 ms

rows.step: Turns it into a tap or a swipe
rows.by: a tap is read as an S2 click; a swipe changes the look
